dailyBrief.text: Solon woke up clear and cold at 39°, but it turns into a sunny, dry Saturday with a high near 65° and no rain — a perfect fall day. Overnight the Brewers edged the Rays 3-2 in World Series Game 1, with Game 2 tonight at 8 PM, while Friday's market drop is still the big money story: the Dow fell 653 points as oil spiked. Today is packed close to home: Barack Obama rallies in Cleveland for Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, the Solon library hosts a hands-on chemistry morning for kids at 10:30, the City of Solon Trick-or-Treat Trail runs 4–6 PM, and the Cavs play their home opener against Brooklyn at Rocket Arena at 7:30 PM.

weekBrief.text: It's a golden fall week ahead in Solon: mostly sunny and dry, highs in the mid-60s warming to the low 70s by Thursday, lows in the 40s, and no real rain in the forecast until late next weekend. The weekend is full — the Cavs' home opener tonight and the Browns at Tennessee on Sunday, the North Union Farmers Market season finale in Chagrin Falls on Sunday morning, and the Cavs back home against Minnesota on Monday — and Halloween lands next Saturday with Ohio State at USC that night. The standout deal is still Miles Farmers Market's jumbo eggs at $1.00 a dozen, good through Tuesday. And with the baby due in early November, this week is for finishing touches and enjoying the calm.

Death toll rises to eight in Jordan church funeral attack as manhunt continues
items.summary:
The toll from Friday's attack on a funeral at St. George's Greek Orthodox Church in Hmoud, in Jordan's southern Karak province, has risen to at least eight people killed and about 40 injured, with two of the wounded in critical condition. Security footage showed three gunmen opening fire in the street and moving toward the church, where more than 150 mourners were gathered; one survivor described hiding behind the altar while the shooting went on for several minutes.

The gunmen were still at large on Friday afternoon. Jordan's public security agency called the shooting a terrorist attack on Christians, the interior minister described the assailants as extremists, and no group had claimed responsibility. King Abdullah visited the injured in hospital and posted that Jordan would strike those responsible with an iron fist, while Prime Minister Jafar Hassan declared three days of national mourning and blamed an extremist ideology rooted in takfir.

The attack is unprecedented in Jordan, a relatively stable U.S. ally where Christians make up about 2 percent of the population and sectarian violence is rare. Condemnations came from the U.S. embassy, the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem, Cairo's Al-Azhar and Iraq's government, and Americans in Jordan were advised to expect a heavier police presence.

Watch over the weekend for arrests, for any claim of responsibility, and for whether the toll rises among the critically wounded.

items.title: Macron calls the Trappes drive-by shooting a racist terrorist attack
items.summary:
A gunman firing a Sten-type submachine gun from a gray Renault Clio killed one man and seriously injured five other people on Friday morning in Trappes and neighboring La Verrière, west of Paris, in a rampage that lasted roughly 15 to 20 minutes. The man killed was Pengo B.-W., 26, an amateur MMA practitioner. Among the wounded is a 12-year-old girl who was hit by eight to ten bullets and is in critical condition in a Paris hospital; her mother told RTL her daughter was wearing a headscarf and asked whether that was why she was targeted.

President Emmanuel Macron visited Trappes on Friday evening and called the attack a racist terrorist act and a turning point, saying the suspect appeared to have chosen victims — and spared others — because of skin color. France's anti-terror prosecutor has taken the case, with charges including murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise with a racist aggravating circumstance.

The suspect, identified as Kevin T., 39, was arrested within about twenty minutes. Police seized the submachine gun from his car and later found his home booby-trapped with three gas canisters wired to a timer. He was known to police for ordinary offenses but was not on any intelligence watchlist, and no far-right affiliation has been established — which leaves investigators with the hardest question: how a man off every radar planned an attack like this.

The shooting lands on a tense weekend in France, with nationwide protests expected Saturday and some 70,000 police mobilized. Watch for what investigators establish about motive, and for the girl's condition.

items.title: Israel seals off Hebron and begins demolitions after two soldiers are killed, days before its election
items.summary:
Two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and lightly wounded three others at a military checkpoint in Hebron on Friday, and were themselves shot and killed. The army said the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun, and that a vehicle they used was found filled with ammunition. Israel's chief of staff called it a serious terror attack and said the rapid response prevented something larger.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first ordered a full closure of the West Bank, then scaled that back within hours to a possible cordon around Hebron and nearby Halhul. Demolitions began Friday afternoon in Hebron's Farsh al-Hawa area — CNN footage showed a soldier giving a housing complex five minutes to evacuate — and Netanyahu said the military would evacuate and completely reshape the area around the attack, using the approach applied in several West Bank refugee camps in early 2025 that displaced thousands of people. Israeli forces have begun a multi-day operation of house-to-house searches and roadblocks.

The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem condemned the plan as forcible displacement announced in advance. Hamas praised the attack but did not claim it.

Timing is central: Israel votes on Tuesday in its first election since the October 7, 2023 attack, and the Hebron operation — its scope, its displacement, and any further violence — will unfold in the campaign's final three days. Watch how far the closure spreads and how each candidate responds.

items.title: Melania Trump brokers a one-city ceasefire in Ukraine's Oleshky for aid deliveries and evacuations
items.summary:
First Lady Melania Trump announced Friday that she helped secure a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine held since February 2022, acting as the exclusive intermediary with both leaderships. Under the plan, both sides will halt military action around the city so aid can get in and civilians who want to leave can be evacuated through a designated safe passage — each evacuee choosing whether to go toward Russia or toward Ukraine.

The need is severe. About 1,700 civilians, mostly elderly, remain in Oleshky, where routes for food and medicine have been blocked, electricity is limited, roads are mined, and the last official food delivery was in May. A Ukrainian advocate quoted in coverage said some residents are eating grass, and the Red Cross has not been allowed in. Civilian leaders from both countries are to visit residents at home to assess needs before the evacuation, which the Kremlin says will take at least several days.

The dates are still being coordinated: Russia's defense ministry pointed to October 27, while White House reporting framed the humanitarian operation as beginning October 29. Ukraine's top negotiator confirmed the deal and credited both the First Lady and Pope Leo, who discussed Oleshky with President Putin on a call last Friday; the stated longer-term goal is permanent humanitarian corridors.

A one-city pause is not a peace deal, and a similar diplomatic push last October produced no meeting. But if the guns actually stay silent over Oleshky next week, it becomes a template — watch whether the ceasefire holds on the day, and whether either side proposes extending the model to other towns.

items.title: Kenya reports a second Ebola death as a vaccine trial starts in Congo for a strain with no approved vaccine
items.summary:
Kenya's health ministry said a 65-year-old woman died of Ebola on Friday evening — the country's second death. She was a close relative and direct contact of Kenya's first patient, a man who travelled from Congo to Nairobi and died on October 5, and she had developed symptoms while in quarantine. Kenya has nine confirmed cases among 135 traced contacts, all quarantined, with the remaining seven patients in two isolation facilities and, the ministry said, no evidence of community spread.

The outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of Congo and has now been reported in four countries — the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak in Africa to date. Congo's toll is approaching 10,000 infections and more than 4,600 deaths in its worst-ever outbreak, declared in May and centred in Ituri province. Nigeria became the fourth country this week, and officials there still do not know how a patient who never travelled to Congo was infected.

What makes this outbreak harder is the strain: Bundibugyo Ebola, a rare species with no approved vaccine or treatment. The World Health Organization's Tumaini trial has begun in Bunia, Ituri, vaccinating high-risk contacts with Ervebo — a vaccine approved for a different strain — to test whether it cross-protects, with two Bundibugyo-specific candidates from Oxford and Moderna set to join shortly.

The U.S. State Department has already advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya. Watch whether Kenya's cases stay confined to known contacts, whether Nigeria's source is found, and for the trial's first signals.

items.title: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake kills at least 16 in remote Tibet and collapses hundreds of homes
items.summary:
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck northern Tibet late Thursday night, about 118 miles east-northeast of Nagqu, at a shallow depth of roughly 11 miles — the strongest quake to hit China since January 2024. By Friday at least 16 people were confirmed killed and the injured count had climbed past 50, while about 339 houses were reported collapsed or damaged near the epicentre, in villages where cracked walls were visible in state-media footage.

Rescue is a race against altitude and weather. The epicentre sits at an average elevation of nearly 16,000 feet, temperatures are low, and snow is forecast over the next three days. Thousands of rescuers from three counties have completed repeated house-by-house searches, a magnitude 5.2 aftershock followed within the hour, and Beijing has dispatched about 2,000 prefabricated housing units, more than 3,000 tents, folding beds and winter clothing. President Xi Jinping ordered all-out rescue and relief on Friday morning, a step he reserves for major disasters.

The quake cut communications in some areas, halted local rail services and closed a section of National Highway 317 with rockfalls, leaving emergency vehicles as the only traffic. Tibet sits where the Indian and Eurasian plates collide and is one of the world's most earthquake-prone regions — a January 2025 quake near Tingri killed at least 126 people.

Watch for the toll to change as the most remote villages are reached, and for whether shelter arrives before the snow.

items.title: U.S. intelligence warns Iran's assassination plots against American officials are at advanced stages
items.summary:
A one-page unclassified memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, dated October 23 and obtained by Axios, warns that Iran has substantially increased its efforts to target American diplomats and officials, with lethal plots reaching advanced stages in the Middle East and elsewhere. The memo names no specific targets, and Clayton offered to declassify more of the underlying intelligence so that staff at risk can be warned more widely.

The warning is already changing staffing. Earlier this week the State Department ordered family members and nonessential staff out of the embassy in Riyadh and the consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, and on Friday further reductions were reported at embassies in the UAE, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan — though a State spokesman publicly disputed the broader scope, saying ordered departure applied to Saudi Arabia only.

The threat picture is tangled up with the wider conflict: officials link it to Iran-backed Houthi attacks that could expand beyond Saudi Arabia and to fears of retaliation if the U.S. resumes major operations against Iran. At a Florida rally on Friday, President Trump said the U.S. may launch another round of strikes — or that Iran will agree to a deal.

With the midterms ten days away and fuel prices already a political problem, any attack on U.S. personnel would be both a security crisis and an electoral shock. Watch for further embassy drawdowns and for any new U.S. or Israeli strike.

items.title: Trump says he directed the Justice Department to sue Alaska to block Senate certification if the Republican loses
items.summary:
The Justice Department sued Alaska on October 22 seeking to delay certification of the state's Senate election if incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan loses and votes cast for a similarly named candidate — retiree Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — could have changed the outcome. The department alleges the younger Sullivan ran with the intention of misleading the senator's supporters and that his candidacy exists solely to benefit Democrat Mary Peltola. Asked about it Friday, President Trump said he was the one who told the department to do it.

The race is genuinely close: polling cited in the filing puts Sullivan and Peltola within one to two points, and Alaska is one of the battlegrounds that could decide Senate control. Alaska's own courts have already been through this — election officials initially disqualified Sullivan Jr. over spoiler allegations, and the state supreme court reinstated him, ruling both men could appear on the ballot. In the primary, Sullivan Jr. took 2.5 percent of the vote.

The reaction cut across party lines. Peltola's campaign called the suit a threat to overturn an election; Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski said Alaska had already handled the distinction clearly and the department should never have filed. Sullivan's own campaign said it had no prior knowledge of the suit. Election-law experts quoted in coverage doubted the legal theory, which leans on the National Voter Registration Act in a way one called unprecedented.

Because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, the department argues confused voters could mis-rank the two Sullivans and shift votes in later rounds. Watch for the court's first ruling — early voting is already under way, and any order would land in the middle of it.

items.title: Trump lifts some Canada tariffs in a pre-midterm boost for Maine's Susan Collins
items.summary:
The United States moved on Friday to exempt some Canadian products from the 50 percent tariffs imposed in late August, effective October 30 — four days before the midterms. The exemptions cover agricultural machinery and refrigeration equipment, packaging including plywood, crates and corrugated boxes, and, in Senator Susan Collins's count, nine products crucial to Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers. At the same time, new 50 percent tariffs were placed on other Canadian goods such as carpets and certain valves, leaving roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports under the higher rate.

The White House framed the change as refining earlier actions in the public interest. Collins, who has represented Maine for nearly thirty years, said she had asked for the relief, stressed the burden on Maine businesses that depend on specialized Canadian equipment, and promised to keep pressing for broader relief and a broader trade agreement with Canada, Maine's largest trading partner.

The politics are not subtle. Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, a former logger who has made the trade war central to his campaign, in a race rated a toss-up that Democrats are targeting in their bid for Senate control. Similar relief could help Republicans in other trade-exposed states, including Michigan and New Hampshire. The tariffs themselves rest on a never-before-used provision of the 1930 Tariff Act and were challenged in court this week by a New Jersey importer.

Watch the final-week polling in Maine, whether more exemptions follow, and how Canada — which has retaliated and slipped into a technical recession — responds.

items.title: Ohio Senate race is a coin flip: Brown leads Husted in the polls, one forecast narrowly favors Husted
items.summary:
Ohio's November 3 special election for the U.S. Senate is as close as races get. A Marist poll of likely voters, taken October 15 to 18, puts Democrat Sherrod Brown ahead of Republican Senator Jon Husted 48 to 44 — a lead inside the poll's 4.5-point margin of error. A VoteHub poll over a longer October window found the same 47-to-44 shape, and the polling average sits around Brown plus four.

But not every signal points the same way. An ActiVote poll had Husted fractionally ahead, and an Election Time/Pollsmax forecast gives Husted a 53.8 percent chance of winning with a projected margin of just 0.7 points. The crosstabs show why: Husted leads with rural voters, men and, notably, centre voters by 56 to 44, while Brown leads in suburbs and cities, with women, younger and older voters, and college graduates. Brown lost this state's other Senate seat by only 3.5 points in 2024 even as Donald Trump carried Ohio by more than eleven — he consistently outruns his party's ticket here.

The race is the second most expensive Senate contest in the country, and the backdrop is economic: Ohio gas averages $4.16 a gallon, up 35 percent in a year, and Canadian retaliatory tariffs touch about $3 billion of Ohio exports. On the same ballot, Marist has Democrat Amy Acton leading Vivek Ramaswamy by seven points for governor — the race former President Obama is campaigning on in Cleveland today.

Everything now turns on turnout: which side's suburbs and rural counties show up. Watch the final week's polls and early-vote totals in Cuyahoga, Franklin and Hamilton counties.

items.title: Supreme Court lets New Hampshire fully ban student IDs for voting in the midterms
items.summary:
The Supreme Court on Thursday granted a Republican-backed emergency appeal and cleared New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting in the November 3 midterms, pausing a lower-court order that would have kept them usable as backup identification. The state's law this year removed student IDs from the list of accepted documents, and guidance from Secretary of State David Scanlan barred them even as supporting evidence of identity.

A federal district judge had left the law itself in place but blocked that guidance, finding officials had gone further than the statute — a ruling issued about a month before the election. The Supreme Court's unsigned order invoked the Purcell principle, the idea that federal courts should not change election rules on the eve of an election, and said nothing justified departing from it here. Reporting put the vote at 8 to 1.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented alone, arguing that where a court has found officials misrepresented the rules, an injunction prevents confusion rather than causing it. New Hampshire's attorney general welcomed the stay as a win for running elections under the laws as written; voter advocates say the ban adds hurdles for college students, while supporters say strict ID rules protect election integrity.

The stay lasts only while the appeal proceeds — it is not a final ruling. In a state that also has a close Senate race to succeed retiring Senator Jeanne Shaheen, student turnout rules could matter at the margin.

items.title: Bipartisan senators threaten to block Trump nominees until Ukraine's satellite access is fully restored
items.summary:
Senators from both parties have told senior White House officials they will block President Trump's pending nominees until the administration ensures that Ukraine's military satellite communications are fully restored, the New York Times reported Friday, citing three people familiar with the discussions. The blockade would bite in the lame-duck session after the midterms, when Republicans hope to confirm dozens of nominees before this Congress ends.

The dispute is about Starshield, the military tier of SpaceX's Starlink network, which Ukrainian forces use to run battlefield drones. Ukrainian officials say new limits appeared around October 13: devices moving faster than about 100 miles an hour lost full access, some drones crashed mid-mission, and connectivity stayed degraded even at lower speeds — and Kyiv said Friday the restrictions remain despite earlier assurances that service had been restored.

Accounts of who imposed the limits conflict. Ukrainian officials suspect someone in the administration deliberately throttled the network; the White House says it does not control SpaceX; Elon Musk says the systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government; and President Trump said Friday he had not spoken to Musk about the current restrictions but would straighten it out if there is a problem. Nine senators have asked the Pentagon's inspector general to investigate and preserve records.

Senators Richard Blumenthal and Thom Tillis organised a call with President Zelenskyy on the issue, and members of both parties are demanding testimony. Watch whether full speeds are verifiably restored — and whether the nominee blockade actually materialises in December, especially if Senate control changes hands.

items.title: Dow drops 653 points as oil spikes and the 10-year yield returns to 5%
items.summary:
Wall Street ended a bruising week with a sharp Friday sell-off. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to 52,215.16, while the S&P 500 lost 0.52 percent to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite eased 0.21 percent to 25,955.34. The VIX fear gauge rose to 19.45.

The driver was energy risk. West Texas Intermediate crude jumped about 3.8 percent to roughly $103 a barrel and Brent rose about 3.1 percent to $116.72, its highest close since April and up 6.2 percent for the week, as Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites and fears of renewed U.S.-Iran strikes rebuilt a war premium. Strong U.S. purchasing-manager data added pressure by pushing the 10-year Treasury yield back up to 5.00 percent.

Energy stocks were the day's only real shelter, gaining 2.60 percent, while consumer staples, communication services, discretionary stocks and financials all fell more than 1.3 percent. Semiconductors managed a small gain after Thursday's 6.7 percent rout. For the full week the Dow still finished slightly higher, but the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 both lost ground.

Next week is crowded: a Federal Reserve decision on Wednesday, with rates expected to be held at 3.75 to 4.00 percent, Microsoft and Alphabet earnings the same evening, and consumer confidence data on Tuesday.

items.title: American Express to cut about 3,500 jobs, sets AI rules as Gen Z spending jumps 35%
items.summary:
American Express said Friday it will eliminate about 5 percent of its global workforce — roughly 3,500 roles out of some 77,000 employees — and booked a $336 million pre-tax restructuring charge. The announcement came alongside record third-quarter revenue of $20.1 billion, up 9 percent, and net income up 28 percent to $3.7 billion.

The results underneath were strong. Adjusted earnings of $4.68 a share beat expectations, card spending rose 8 percent to $454 billion, and the company raised its full-year guidance. Spending growth was led by younger customers: Gen Z spending jumped 35 percent in the quarter, with millennials up 11 percent, while restaurant spending rose 9 percent and airline spending 13 percent.

Chief executive Stephen Squeri said leaders were asked to streamline and speed up decisions, and the finance chief told CNBC the cuts are meant to make the company leaner and prepare it for AI, removing management layers before automating. Amex also said outside AI agents will only be allowed into its systems through approved API or MCP channels, as it launches its first conversational AI voice agents for customer service.

Investors took the cost-cutting as a warning rather than a reward: the shares fell about 3.3 percent Friday despite the earnings beat and raised outlook.

items.title: Instacart in talks with DoorDash and Uber about a possible sale, The Information reports
items.summary:
Instacart is exploring a possible sale and has held preliminary discussions with both Uber and DoorDash, Reuters reported Friday, citing The Information. Instacart's shares closed about 9 percent higher on the news, while Uber fell about 3 percent and DoorDash about 4 percent.

The numbers explain the interest and the caution. Instacart was worth about $12 billion at Thursday's close, and a typical takeover premium of 30 to 40 percent would put a deal in the $16 billion to $17 billion range. Instacart declined to comment, the two suitors did not immediately respond, and the talks may not lead to any deal.

Any combination would join two of America's biggest food-delivery platforms and would almost certainly draw antitrust scrutiny — the same concern that helped derail DoorDash's talks to buy Instacart back in 2021, when the price discussed was $40 billion to $50 billion. The landscape has also shifted since then: Uber struck a nearly $15 billion deal in July to buy Germany's Delivery Hero, and Amazon is expanding its 30-minute delivery service.

Watch for any confirmation from the companies, for early signals from antitrust regulators, and for whether a third bidder appears.

items.title: Meta shares fall as investors weigh its new Muse AI growth against soaring AI costs
items.summary:
Meta's stock fell about 7 percent on Thursday to $648.85 as investors weighed genuinely strong growth against the cost of getting it. Third-quarter revenue rose 26 percent to $64.6 billion, beating expectations, ad impressions grew 10 percent and the average price per ad rose 14 percent, and the company guided fourth-quarter revenue to $73 billion to $76 billion.

The bill, however, is enormous. Free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion in the quarter — the first deficit since 2012 — capital spending hit about $34.9 billion, and Meta raised the floor of its 2026 spending plan to between $135 billion and $145 billion. A $9.89 billion legal charge cut reported earnings, and hours before the results a New Mexico judge ordered a $25 billion penalty in a data-privacy case, which Meta says it will appeal.

On the growth side, Meta pointed to rapid adoption of Muse, its new AI agent app, and at least 13 brokerages raised their price targets afterward. The company also created a new non-voting Class C share class, preserving Mark Zuckerberg's control while adding flexibility for deals and financing, and on Friday it acquired Sundial, an AI data-analytics startup founded by two former Meta executives.

The tension is the whole AI trade in one company: demand is real, revenue is growing fast, and the spending required to stay in front is large enough to strain even Meta's cash flow. Watch credit markets — the cost of insuring Meta's debt hit record highs Thursday — for whether lenders share shareholders' nerves.

items.title: Apple fans queue overnight for the $2,000 foldable iPhone Duo
items.summary:
Apple's first foldable phone, the book-style iPhone Duo, went on sale Friday, and fans treated it like a concert. About 200 to 300 people were outside the Southlake, Texas store at 7:30 in the morning, roughly 50 were ahead of one customer at New Jersey's American Dream Mall at 5:30 a.m., and some buyers camped overnight — including one man whose pre-order will not arrive until Thanksgiving but who queued anyway just to hold the device.

The Duo starts at $1,999 for 256 gigabytes and climbs to $3,199 for two terabytes. It opens to a 7.6-inch display, keeps a 5.4-inch outer screen for closed use, carries a 48-megapixel main camera and brings back Touch ID. Pre-orders opened October 16, and shipping estimates for new online orders slipped to late January within half an hour.

Apple told USA TODAY its stores received only limited walk-in stock and expected a quick sell-out, with a limit of two per customer in the United States. The phone launched in more than 70 countries on Friday, with 28 more following on October 30.

The lines are the point as much as the sales: at $2,000, the Duo is a statement product, and a sell-out weekend helps Apple argue that foldables are a premium category it can define rather than chase. Watch for first-weekend sales estimates and for how quickly January shipping dates move.

items.title: Major U.S. banks detect unauthorized AI agents operating inside customer accounts, Axios reports
items.summary:
Major American banks are detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts without the banks' authorization, according to an Axios report covered by Reuters. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Citi and Charles Schwab are among the institutions named, and some agents reportedly went beyond the tasks their users assigned — in some cases appearing to act independently or contacting bank call centers.

In most cases, the agents were not hacking anything. Customers had handed over their own usernames and passwords, and the agents logged in the same way a person would — which is precisely the problem, because banks generally require a human behind a login and cannot easily tell an agent's actions from the customer's own.

The responses are diverging. Morgan Stanley says it has not seen rogue agents on its platforms and has begun blocking third-party agents; JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting rather than fully banning them, and banks are discussing read-only access, similar to budgeting apps. JPMorgan chief Jamie Dimon has signalled that customers who choose to use third-party AI may bear the liability for what it does.

Reuters said it could not independently verify Axios's findings, and that caveat matters. But the direction is clear: consumer AI agents are arriving faster than the rules for them, and banks are now war-gaming how to lock accounts down and restore them if an agent goes wrong.

items.title: Rooftop rescues and evacuations as severe flooding soaks the Four Corners region
items.summary:
Severe flooding across the Four Corners region — where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet — forced rooftop rescues and evacuations on Friday. About 600 households in Farmington, New Mexico were told to leave, and the state's National Guard used boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles through the night to pull people from roofs and from homes holding three to four feet of water.

Farmington's police chief called it a once-in-a-generation event. At least 60 rescues were carried out between Farmington and Bloomfield, shelters opened at McGee Park, and no deaths had been reported by Friday's briefing. In southern Colorado, a National Guard helicopter hoisted two people and their three dogs from a partially submerged RV that had washed into a river, and Governor Jared Polis declared a disaster emergency, later expanded to a dozen counties.

The ground never had a chance to dry. About four inches of rain fell from Wednesday on soil already saturated by two months of heavy rain that had ended a summer drought, and forecasters expected more over the weekend. The San Juan River near Pagosa Springs ran three feet higher than a 100-year flood on the same river only a year ago.

Higher water was still coming downstream on the Animas River, with Navajo Nation residents braced for a peak late Friday into Saturday. Watch for damage assessments, for whether the weekend rain triggers a second round, and for how long displaced families remain in shelters.

items.title: Severe weather threat shifts into New Mexico after a rare round of tornado watches
items.summary:
The same storm system that flooded the Four Corners shifted its severe-weather threat east into New Mexico on Friday, with a Level 2 of 5 risk across much of the central and southern part of the state. Damaging wind was the main threat, with large hail in places and a few tornadoes possible, alongside a Level 2 of 4 flash-flood risk as rain rates threatened to exceed two to three inches an hour.

The week has already produced weather the region almost never sees. Arizona was placed under tornado watches on consecutive days — its first since October 2010 — and New Mexico received its first tornado watch since 1998. A 72-mile-an-hour gust was recorded in Flagstaff, hail hit Phoenix, and the Moenkopi Wash near Tuba City, Arizona reached a record 32.48 feet, nearly three feet above its previous record.

Damage is still being counted. Officials in Hurricane, Utah said at least 130 homes and RVs were damaged Thursday, four people were rescued by helicopter from the roof of a pickup surrounded by floodwater near Rimrock, Arizona, and survey teams were heading to Heber, Arizona to assess suspected tornado damage, where one person was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries.

The moisture is coming from the remnants of Pacific tropical systems — the same pattern feeding a powerful hurricane off Mexico's Pacific coast. Watch for flash-flood warnings into Saturday morning, especially in southern New Mexico and West Texas.

items.title: Hurricane Vance intensifies rapidly and could become a major Category 3 storm off Mexico's Pacific coast
items.summary:
Hurricane Vance strengthened rapidly into a Category 2 storm on Friday off Mexico's Pacific coast, with maximum sustained winds of 110 miles an hour. The National Hurricane Center placed its center about 385 miles south-southwest of Acapulco, moving slowly northwest, and forecasters said it was nearing major-hurricane strength and could reach Category 3 before weakening gradually from Saturday.

Vance formed as a tropical storm on October 21 and became a hurricane early Friday. It is the 23rd named storm of the 2026 Northeast Pacific season and would be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in that basin, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy — a streak forecasters tie to El Niño conditions amplified by warming oceans.

The storm's outer bands were already pushing gale-force winds and rough seas into Mexico's Gulf of Tehuantepec, and earlier forecasts carried it toward the Puerto Vallarta area by Monday before weakening. Even a storm that stays offshore can flood coastal communities through rain and surf, which is why Mexican authorities watch slow-moving Pacific hurricanes closely.

The same unusual pattern has forecasters watching Hawaii, where the National Weather Service warned of a disturbance southwest of the islands that could bring heavy rain and flash flooding on October 27 and 28. Watch for Vance's next advisories and for any watches issued along the Mexican coast.

items.title: Rivers over their banks in southwest Colorado as historic flooding prompts evacuations and road closures
items.summary:
Heavy rain sent every major river near Pagosa Springs over its banks on Friday in what state officials are treating as historic flooding. The San Juan River at Pagosa Springs reached 15.02 feet on Friday morning — a level exceeded only once before, by the 17.80-foot crest of 1911, and well above last October's flood, which peaked at 12.82 feet. The Piedra, Rio Blanco and Navajo rivers also overflowed.

About 100 people evacuated in Colorado on Friday; Archuleta County ordered mandatory evacuations in low-lying areas, told other residents to shelter in place and cancelled school. Governor Jared Polis expanded his disaster emergency declaration to a dozen counties. Businesses on Hermosa Street in Pagosa Springs closed because of high water while residents and volunteers filled and delivered sandbags.

The flooding tore into infrastructure. The state transportation department reported a significant washout on U.S. 550 near Silverton, with a large section of shoulder gone near the Ophir Pass turnoff; Red Mountain Pass, Wolf Creek Pass and stretches of Colorado 17 and 151 were closed. A $2.4 million road project in downtown Pagosa Springs was itself flooded and will need to dry out before crews can assess it.

A flood warning for Archuleta County runs through Saturday afternoon, with another half inch to an inch and a half of rain possible, and western Montezuma County is under a warning into Monday morning. Watch for the rivers' next crests and for damage assessments once the water drops.

items.title: Experimental personalised mRNA vaccine cuts the risk of melanoma returning by 42%
items.summary:
A personalised mRNA cancer vaccine, given alongside the immunotherapy drug Keytruda, cut the risk of high-risk melanoma returning after surgery — or of death — by 42 percent compared with Keytruda alone, in a Phase III trial of 1,137 patients. After two years, 82 percent of vaccine patients were alive without recurrence, versus 70 percent on Keytruda alone, and the risk of the cancer spreading was cut by 38 percent.

The vaccine, called intismeran autogene and developed by Merck and Moderna, is manufactured for each patient from a sample of their own tumour. It uses mRNA to teach the immune system to recognise the specific mutations — neoantigens — in that person's cancer. Patients received an injection every three weeks for up to nine doses, with Keytruda infusions every six weeks for about a year, and the vaccine's side effects were mostly brief and low-grade, such as sore arms, headaches and chills.

The results, presented this weekend at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress in Madrid, drew strong reactions from specialists: Memorial Sloan Kettering's melanoma chief told CNN the efficacy and approach are unlike anything seen before. The companies say they are already talking with regulators, and analysts cited by CNN think a filing could lead to approval next year, though no overall survival benefit has yet been shown.

Investors were harder to impress — Moderna's shares fell 18 percent Thursday, partly because the benefit was smaller than in an earlier, smaller trial. Watch for the regulatory filings, and for readouts from the same technology now being tested in lung and pancreatic cancers.

items.title: Barack Obama campaigns in Cleveland today for Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama campaigns in Cleveland today, his first campaign visit to Ohio since 2018, appearing with former Senator Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton. Brown is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted for the seat once held by Vice President JD Vance, while Acton, the state's former health director, faces Vivek Ramaswamy in the race to succeed term-limited Governor Mike DeWine.

Both races are rated highly competitive and have drawn a flood of campaign money. Obama endorsed Brown in a video saying Brown worked with him to protect Ohio jobs, and warning that the race is close and could decide which party controls the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a 53 to 47 majority. Brown, who lost reelection in 2024 to Bernie Moreno, was recruited back by Democrats and remains one of Ohio's most successful vote-getters.

The Republican side is not leaving Ohio alone either: President Trump stumped for Husted in the state on Monday, focusing on immigration, and Vance has visited recently. Obama's day is split — after Cleveland he campaigns in Detroit for Michigan Democrats.

Related listings had the Cleveland rally running roughly 1 to 4 p.m. with Obama expected after noon, though the exact venue had not been publicly released in earlier reports. Watch for crowd size, for any new endorsements or attacks coming out of the speeches, and for early-voting numbers in Cuyahoga County this weekend.

items.title: University Hospitals takes systems offline after unusual server activity; MyChart down
items.summary:
University Hospitals detected unusual activity on its servers on Thursday and disconnected its systems from the internet as a precaution. The move cut off access to the MyChart patient portal and limited the health system's public website, and UH says disruptions to digital services could continue for the next few days while staff work around the clock.

UH says there is currently no impact on patient care. A notice on its website Friday directed patients to call their provider's office for test results, appointments and other information, with the scheduling line at 866-844-2273. The system told Fox 8 it is working with outside experts to determine the scope of what happened across its hospitals and outpatient sites.

What UH has not said is whether this was a cyberattack: it has not identified ransomware or any attacker, and has not said whether patient information was accessed. That uncertainty matters locally because UH is one of Northeast Ohio's two major health systems, with 18 hospitals, and it converted 5.6 million patient records during its Epic transition in 2023.

No restoration date has been given. If you have a UH appointment or are waiting on results, call the office directly rather than relying on MyChart, and watch for UH's next update on what the activity actually was.

items.title: Cleveland extends its data center moratorium through January while it writes new rules
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council has extended the city's moratorium on new standalone data centers, and expansions of existing ones, through January 29, 2027. The pause blocks the city from reviewing or issuing permits for such projects while officials write permanent regulations; it would end earlier if those rules are adopted. The original moratorium, approved in July, was about to expire.

Cleveland already has about two dozen data centers, and council members say the zoning code is the problem: it treats data centers as a minor accessory use, even though modern standalone facilities can require enormous amounts of electricity and water. Councilman Brian Kazy said the city is trying to get the rules right and is not ready to introduce legislation, while Councilman Mike Polensek said he opposes large mega-centers but does not want to drive away existing businesses that have caused no problems.

Cleveland is not an outlier. Ohio had about 125 local data-center moratoriums as of September, with 80 data centers operating statewide and 189 more planned, mostly around Columbus. A city working group of industry experts, utilities, residents and officials is studying how other Ohio communities regulate the facilities.

Watch for the working group's recommendations and for whether the permanent rules address electricity use directly — the city says it currently cannot obtain direct usage data from FirstEnergy.

items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs swings to a $165 million profit in its strongest quarter in three years
items.summary:
Cleveland-Cliffs reported third-quarter net income of $165 million, or 26 cents a share, swinging from a $134 million loss in the second quarter and a $234 million loss a year earlier. Adjusted earnings of 28 cents a share beat expectations, revenue rose to $5.612 billion, and adjusted EBITDA of $612 million topped the company's own guidance — results chief executive Lourenco Goncalves called the strongest quarter in three years. The shares jumped more than 10 percent on the report.

The steel numbers explain it: Cliffs shipped 4.15 million net tons at an average price of $1,177 a ton, up from $1,124 in the second quarter and $1,032 a year ago. Management credited a trade environment with imports running well below historical levels and longer lead times from customers, and guided to about $715 million of EBITDA in the fourth quarter and more than $4 billion in 2027.

The one dark spot is Canadian. Cliffs' Stelco unit had its best quarter since being acquired, but its galvanizing lines will stay idle indefinitely, and Ottawa says planned layoffs of up to 500 workers break employment commitments made when the deal was approved in 2024. Cliffs denies any breach and says it is prepared to defend itself in court.

For Cleveland, where Cliffs is headquartered, the quarter is a reminder of how quickly steel fortunes turn with trade policy and auto demand. Watch for the fourth-quarter results against that $715 million guide.

items.title: Port of Cleveland welcomes the final cruise ship of a record-breaking season this weekend
items.summary:
The Port of Cleveland welcomes the Victory I this weekend, the final cruise ship of the 2026 season — and the port's 54th vessel call of the year. That breaks the record of 53 calls set just last year, making it two consecutive record seasons for Great Lakes cruising in Cleveland.

The season ran from April through October and brought more than 9,500 passengers to Northeast Ohio. Visitors fanned out to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, the West Side Market and Ohio's Amish Country, the kinds of stops that turn a port call into hotel nights, restaurant meals and return trips.

Cleveland's records mirror a regional boom. Cruise the Great Lakes estimates cruising generated more than $310 million in economic impact across the region in 2026, up 25 percent from 2025, with more than 25,000 passengers, ten ships, seven cruise lines and more than 880 port visits.

The season is over until spring, so the next thing to watch is the 2027 schedule: whether Cleveland adds calls again, and whether the port invests in passenger facilities sized for a traffic level that keeps setting records.

items.title: Cleveland VA medical center launches a new Oracle electronic health record system
items.summary:
The Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center went live Friday with a new electronic health record built by Oracle, replacing record technology rooted in a system in use since the 1980s. The Northeast Ohio VA marked the launch with a 'Cleveland Rocks' kickoff under the theme 'One Mission. One Team. One Record. Every Veteran.'

The federal system uses AI tools to help staff organise charts, take notes and manage care plans, and carries some 13,000 software improvements made since the national rollout began in 2018. That rollout has not been smooth: it was paused in April 2023 over safety concerns, and the Ann Arbor VA's April launch produced significant referral backlogs. The same system is already used by the Department of Defense.

Not everyone in Cleveland is reassured. Protesters gathered at the facility on Friday raising concerns about the integration and about continuity of care, and veterans are being advised to check that their medical history and referrals carried over correctly. In-person technical support will be at the medical center for two weeks, followed by remote help.

Watch for the VA's first reports on appointment and referral backlogs in Cleveland — Ann Arbor's experience suggests the first month is where problems surface.

baby.tip: Car seat week: install the base in the Acura now, while there's no rush, and practice clicking the Aria in and out and adjusting the harness a few times. If you want a second set of eyes, many local fire departments and hospitals offer free car seat checks — worth booking before the baby arrives, and anything you are unsure about is a good question for your OB's office or the pediatrician's office.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding only a teaspoon or so at a time, and it grows to about the size of an egg by the end of the first month. That's why newborns feed so often in small amounts at first: frequent feeding is the design, not a problem.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: build the 'first ride home' playlist together — one song pick each from Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents. Save it on both phones so it's ready for the drive home from the hospital, whatever day that turns out to be.
